facts: The Samuel Butler Room was founded in 1960 as the society for St John's postgraduates.
Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon, was at St John's from 1854 to 1858.
The SBR room is at I2 First Court: TV with a Wii, board games, a pool table, a piano and a kitchen.
Port & Sherry runs on Fridays after hall, GBP1.50 a glass.
BA Table runs on Tuesdays and Fridays in full term.
The SBR swaps formal halls with Balliol, Trinity College Dublin, Ghislieri and Uppsala.
The Graduate Student Residence (GSR) is at 1 All Saints Passage.
Grad talks happen before BA Table, and there is a research symposium in Lent.
Samuel Butler was born on 4 December 1835 at the rectory in Langar, Nottinghamshire.
Butler's grandfather, Dr Samuel Butler, was headmaster of Shrewsbury School and later Bishop of Lichfield.
Butler graduated from St John's with first-class honours in Classics in 1858.
Butler sailed to New Zealand on the Roman Emperor, arriving at Lyttelton on 27 January 1860.
Butler ran Mesopotamia Station for about four years and went home with double his GBP8,000 investment.
The title Erewhon is an anagram of 'nowhere'.
In Erewhon, illness is treated as a crime and crime as an illness.
Erewhon's jailer's daughter Yram is 'Mary' spelled backwards.
Butler's 1863 letter 'Darwin among the Machines' in Christchurch's The Press was signed 'Cellarius'.
The Butlerian Jihad against thinking machines in Dune is named after Samuel Butler.
Alan Turing wrote that machines might 'take control' in the way mentioned in Butler's Erewhon.
The Way of All Flesh was published in 1903, the year after Butler died.
The Modern Library ranked The Way of All Flesh 12th among the 20th century's best English-language novels.
In Erewhon Revisited, Erewhonians worship Higgs as 'the Sunchild' after his balloon escape.
Butler's Shrewsbury headmaster, Benjamin Hall Kennedy, inspired Dr Skinner in The Way of All Flesh.
Edoras scenes for The Lord of the Rings were filmed in the Rangitata valley, Butler's old stomping ground.
Butler fell out bitterly with Charles Darwin over Darwin's 1879 Life of Erasmus Darwin.
In Evolution, Old and New, Butler argued Darwin had not fairly credited Buffon, Lamarck and Erasmus Darwin.
Butler argued the Odyssey was written by a young Sicilian woman from around Trapani.
Robert Graves turned Butler's Odyssey theory into the novel Homer's Daughter.
Butler's prose translations of the Iliad (1898) and Odyssey (1900) are still consulted today.
Henry Festing Jones gave up the law to be Butler's assistant and travelling companion for GBP200 a year.
Butler and Jones wrote Narcissus, a cantata in the style of Handel, published in 1888.
Jones's 1919 Memoir of Butler won the very first James Tait Black Prize for biography.
The Sacro Monte at Varallo, subject of Butler's Ex Voto, was founded in 1491 and has 45 chapels.
Varallo's Sacro Monte holds over 800 life-size painted statues in wood and terracotta.
Erasmus Darwin turned down George III's offer to be Physician to the King.
Trapani's name comes from the Greek for sickle, after the curve of its harbour.
Charles Darwin studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, finishing tenth of 178 candidates.
Peterhouse, founded in 1284 by Hugh de Balsham, Bishop of Ely, is the oldest Cambridge college.
Robinson, founded in 1977, is the newest of the 31 Cambridge colleges.
Peterhouse was the first Cambridge college with electric lighting, installed by Lord Kelvin in 1883-84.
King's College Chapel has the world's largest fan vault, built by John Wastell between 1512 and 1515.
Rubens painted The Adoration of the Magi, above the King's Chapel altar, in 1634 for a convent in Louvain.
The Corpus Clock's grasshopper is the Chronophage, or time eater, unveiled by Stephen Hawking in 2008.
The Corpus Clock is only exactly right about once every five minutes.
The Mathematical Bridge at Queens' was built in 1749, 22 years after Newton died, so he cannot have built it.
Trinity's Great Court clock strikes each hour twice, said to be once for Trinity and once for St John's.
Harold Abrahams, shown attempting the Great Court Run in Chariots of Fire, never actually tried it.
Pepys left over 3,000 books to Magdalene, arranged by size; none may be sold and none added.
Magdalene was the last all-male college in Oxford or Cambridge to admit women, in 1988.
In 1958 Caius engineering students put an Austin Seven van on the roof of the Senate House.
Students began taking tea in the apple orchard at Grantchester in 1897.
Grantchester is said to have the world's highest concentration of Nobel Prize winners.
One of the 14 stone balls on Clare Bridge, built in 1639-40, is missing a section.
Jesus College's symbol is the cockerel, a play on the surname of its founder, John Alcock.
Caius students pass through the Gates of Humility, Virtue and Honour during their time at college.
Henry VIII's statue on Trinity's Great Gate holds a chair leg in place of his sceptre, thanks to pranksters.
Pembroke has the first chapel designed by Christopher Wren, consecrated in 1665.
Cambridge, Massachusetts, was first called Newtowne and was renamed in 1638 after the University of Cambridge.
John Harvard studied at Emmanuel; his 1638 bequest of about 400 books gave Harvard College its name.
Gates Cambridge Scholarships began in 2000, funded by the Gates Foundation, for graduate applicants from outside the UK.
Two prime ministers of New Zealand, Alfred Domett and Sir Francis Bell, were Johnians.
Cambridge, New Zealand, on the Waikato River, is known as the Town of Trees and Champions.
Lee Kuan Yew (Fitzwilliam) and his son Lee Hsien Loong (Trinity) both led Singapore.
Johnian Richard Cockburn Maclaurin was president of MIT from 1909 to 1920.
Three Johnians served as British prime minister in the 1800s: Goderich, Aberdeen and Palmerston.
Johnian Nagendra Singh was President of the International Court of Justice from 1985 to 1988.
Butler went to Canada in 1874 to try to save a failing tanning company.
St John's received its charter on 9 April 1511 and is named after St John the Evangelist.
The college stands on the site of the Hospital of St John the Evangelist, probably founded around 1200.
Lady Margaret Beaufort died without mentioning the college in her will; John Fisher secured its founding.
John Fisher was executed by Henry VIII in 1535 and canonised alongside Thomas More in 1935.
The School of Pythagoras, built around 1200, is the oldest secular building in Cambridge.
Merton College, Oxford owned the School of Pythagoras from 1266 until 1959.
Queen Elizabeth I rode on horseback into the St John's Hall in 1564.
New Court, built 1826 to 1831, is nicknamed The Wedding Cake and has four blank clock faces.
The Chapel tower, 163 ft tall and modelled on Pershore Abbey, was left without bells.
In 1963 students hoisted a 1928 Austin 7 under the Bridge of Sighs.
Queen Victoria called the Bridge of Sighs so pretty and picturesque.
The scarlet jackets of Lady Margaret Boat Club gave rise to the word blazer.
Lady Margaret Boat Club, founded in 1825, is the oldest boat club in the university.
The St John's May Ball was first held in 1888, and its theme stays secret until the night.
Shrewsbury Tower in Third Court housed an observatory from 1765 to 1859.
The college motto, Souvent me Souvient, is a triple pun in Old French.
Johnian John Herschel coined the word photography, and fellow Johnian Fred Hoyle coined the term Big Bang.
St John's choir was reportedly the first in the UK to webcast its services, starting in 2008.
St John's first admitted women in October 1981, and the first women undergraduates arrived a year later.
The river is called the Granta above Silver Street Bridge and the Cam below it.
The Cam's name was back-formed from Grantebrycge, the Old English name for Cambridge.
The Cam joins the Great Ouse at Pope's Corner, just south of Ely.
The Olympic torch was punted down the Cam during the 2012 torch relay.
Cambridge punters stand on the till; Oxford punters stand at the other end, inside the boat.
The first Boat Race was rowed at Henley-on-Thames in 1829, and Oxford won easily.
The 1877 Boat Race was declared a dead heat, with both crews timed at 24 minutes 8 seconds.
Both crews sank in the 1912 Boat Race, and the race was abandoned.
The narrowest Boat Race win was 1 foot (Oxford, 2003); the widest was 35 lengths (Cambridge, 1839).
Cambridge won 13 men's Boat Races in a row, from 1924 to 1936.
The 2021 Boat Races were held on the Great Ouse at Ely instead of the Thames.
Cambridge's reserve crews are Goldie and Blondie; Oxford's are Isis and Osiris.
The first attested bumps race was in Oxford in 1815, between Brasenose and Jesus College eights.
Bump up on all four days and you win blades; get bumped on all four and you get spoons.
King John granted Cambridge's Midsummer Fair a charter in 1211.
At 100 yards, the Jesus Green lido is among the longest outdoor swimming pools in Europe.
Jesus Green was split from Midsummer Common in 1890, when Victoria Avenue was built.
Henley Royal Regatta was founded on 26 March 1839 at a public meeting in Henley town hall.
The word coxswain literally means boat servant, from cockboat plus swain.
On 28 February 1953 Francis Crick told drinkers at The Eagle that he and Watson had found the secret of life.
The Eagle opened in 1667 as a coaching inn, near the Cavendish Laboratory.
WWII airmen wrote on the ceiling of The Eagle's RAF Bar using candles, petrol lighters and lipstick.
The Eagle serves a beer called Eagle's DNA to mark the 1953 discovery.
The Cavendish Laboratory opened in 1874, paid for by the 7th Duke of Devonshire, then university chancellor.
As of 2019, 30 researchers from the Cavendish Laboratory had won Nobel Prizes.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron at the Cavendish Laboratory in 1932.
Footlights was founded in 1883, and its 1981 revue won the first Perrier Award at the Edinburgh Fringe.
In 2006 a visitor tripped and smashed three Qing vases at the Fitzwilliam; museum experts restored them.
The Fitzwilliam Museum was founded in 1816 with a bequest of 100,000 pounds, and admission is always free.
The Botanic Garden recorded 38.7 C on 25 July 2019, a UK temperature record at the time.
A tree grown from Newton's apple tree stood in the Botanic Garden from 1954 until Storm Eunice in 2022.
Isaac Newton was admitted to Trinity in 1661 as a subsizar, paying his way by doing chores.
The FA's first laws of 1863 drew heavily on the Cambridge Rules of football.
Cambridge was granted city status in 1951, though its first town charter dates from the 12th century.
Jim Ede made Kettle's Yard by converting four small cottages into one house, and held open house every afternoon.
Paul Simon was a late addition to the bill of the first Cambridge Folk Festival.
Market Square has been a marketplace since Saxon times and was only cleared after a big fire in 1849.
Cambridge University began around 1209, when scholars left Oxford after a clash with the townspeople.
King Henry III granted Cambridge a royal charter in 1231, 22 years after the university was founded.
Cambridge alumni, academics and affiliates have won more than 120 Nobel Prizes.
Cambridge's 100-plus libraries hold around 16 million books.
During full term students must live within three miles of Great St Mary's, a rule called keeping term.
A Cambridge full term lasts just eight weeks.
May Week is held in June, after exams, despite its name.
The Cambridge Union first met on 13 February 1815, eight years before the Oxford Union existed.
The last wooden spoon went in 1909 to Cuthbert Holthouse, an oarsman of St John's own Lady Margaret Boat Club.
In 1890 Philippa Fawcett topped the Mathematical Tripos and was declared 'above the Senior Wrangler'.
A Cambridge BA can be promoted to MA with no further exams, six years after first coming into residence.
The Tripos may be named after the three-legged stools candidates once sat on during oral exams.
The webcam was reportedly invented at Cambridge to keep an eye on the Trojan Room coffee pot.
Varsity, Cambridge's oldest independent student newspaper, was founded in 1947.
The Senate, made up of everyone holding a Cambridge MA or higher, elects the Chancellor.
Survivors' photos are taken at dawn of May Ball guests who make it through the whole night.
Cambridge and the University of the South are the only universities still using the scarlet cappa clausa.

facts: Sans Frontieres is the SBR's celebration of its members' home countries.

featured.name: United Kingdom
featured.fact: Samuel Butler was born in Langar, Nottinghamshire, schooled at Shrewsbury and studied at St John's, Cambridge.

featured.name: Ireland
featured.fact: Trinity College Dublin, a sister college of St John's, is one of the SBR's formal hall swap partners.

featured.name: Italy
featured.fact: Collegio Ghislieri in Pavia, an SBR swap partner, was founded by Pope Pius V in 1567.

featured.name: Sweden
featured.fact: Uppsala University, an SBR swap partner, was founded in 1477 and is the oldest university in the Nordic countries.

featured.name: New Zealand
featured.fact: Butler ran Mesopotamia Station in Canterbury from 1860 and drew on it for the opening of Erewhon.

featured.name: Canada
featured.fact: In 1874 Butler went to Canada to try to save the Canada Tanning Extract Company.

featured.name: Switzerland
featured.fact: Butler's travel book Alps and Sanctuaries covers Piedmont and the Swiss canton of Ticino.

featured.name: United States
featured.fact: Cambridge, Massachusetts, home of Harvard and MIT, was named in 1638 after the University of Cambridge.

featured.name: Greece
featured.fact: Samuel Butler made prose translations of Homer's Iliad (1898) and Odyssey (1900) that are still read today.

featured.name: Germany
featured.fact: Cambridge has been twinned with the university city of Heidelberg since 1965.

featured.name: Ecuador
featured.fact: Christ's College man Charles Darwin studied finches and tortoises on Ecuador's Galapagos Islands.

featured.name: India
featured.fact: Johnian Manmohan Singh was Prime Minister of India from 2004 to 2014.

featured.name: France
featured.fact: William Waddington, Prime Minister of France in 1879, studied at Trinity, Cambridge.

featured.name: Belgium
featured.fact: Georges Lemaitre, the Belgian priest who proposed the expanding universe, studied at St Edmund's, Cambridge.

featured.name: Netherlands
featured.fact: The Dutch scholar Erasmus taught at Queens' during his stays in Cambridge between 1506 and 1515.

featured.name: Australia
featured.fact: Stanley Bruce, Prime Minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929, studied at Trinity Hall, Cambridge.

featured.name: Pakistan
featured.fact: Choudhary Rahmat Ali, credited with coining the name Pakistan, studied at Emmanuel, Cambridge.

featured.name: Sri Lanka
featured.fact: Dudley Senanayake, three times Prime Minister of Ceylon, studied at Corpus Christi, Cambridge.

featured.name: Malaysia
featured.fact: Tunku Abdul Rahman, Malaysia's first prime minister, studied at St Catharine's, Cambridge.

featured.name: Thailand
featured.fact: Anand Panyarachun, Prime Minister of Thailand in 1991-92, studied at Trinity, Cambridge.

featured.name: Jordan
featured.fact: Awn Al-Khasawneh, Prime Minister of Jordan from 2011 to 2012, studied at Queens', Cambridge.

featured.name: Zambia
featured.fact: Two Zambian presidents, Rupiah Banda and Guy Scott, studied at Cambridge.

featured.name: South Africa
featured.fact: Jan Smuts, twice Prime Minister of South Africa, studied at Christ's College, Cambridge.

featured.name: Lesotho
featured.fact: King Letsie III of Lesotho studied at Wolfson College, Cambridge.

featured.name: Denmark
featured.fact: Queen Margrethe II of Denmark studied archaeology at Girton College, Cambridge.

featured.name: Uganda
featured.fact: Mutesa II and Muwenda Mutebi II, Kabakas of Buganda, both studied at Magdalene, Cambridge.

featured.name: Luxembourg
featured.fact: Luc Frieden, Prime Minister of Luxembourg since 2023, studied at Queens', Cambridge.

featured.name: Trinidad and Tobago
featured.fact: George Maxwell Richards, President of Trinidad and Tobago from 2003 to 2013, studied at Pembroke, Cambridge.

featured.name: Japan
featured.fact: Johnian Kikuchi Dairoku became Japan's Minister of Education and President of Tokyo University.

featured.name: China
featured.fact: The celebrated Chinese novelist Jin Yong earned his PhD at St John's.

featured.name: Nigeria
featured.fact: Johnian Geoffrey Onyeama became Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs in 2015.

featured.name: Russia
featured.fact: Russian physicist Pyotr Kapitsa worked at the Cavendish and was a fellow of Trinity before winning a Nobel Prize.

featured.name: Hungary
featured.fact: Cambridge has been twinned with the Hungarian university city of Szeged since 1987.

featured.name: Argentina
featured.fact: Argentine Nobel laureate Cesar Milstein worked in Cambridge and was a fellow of Darwin College.

featured.name: Israel
featured.fact: Abba Eban, Israel's long-serving foreign minister, studied at Queens' College, Cambridge.

featured.name: Cyprus
featured.fact: Johnian Hugh Foot, a former Cambridge Union president, was the last British Governor of Cyprus.

featured.name: Iran
featured.fact: Johnian Henry Martyn, Senior Wrangler in 1801, translated the New Testament into Persian.

featured.name: Sierra Leone
featured.fact: Sierra Leonean scientist and writer Abioseh Nicol studied at Christ's and became its first African fellow.
